name: Marine Chemistry
tagline: Ocean chemistry, marine natural products, and aquatic geochemistry.
seo_title: Marine Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Marine Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in seawater chemistry, ocean acidification, marine pollution and marine natural products.

definition.lead: Marine chemistry studies the composition of seawater and the chemical processes of the oceans, from dissolved salts and gases to the molecules made by marine life.
definition.body: The ocean absorbs a large share of the CO₂ we emit, which is making it more acidic. Its organisms also produce unusual molecules, some of which have become medicines.

timeline.title: HMS Challenger
timeline.text: The first global oceanographic expedition sets sail (1872–1876).

timeline.title: Constant proportions
timeline.text: William Dittmar analyses Challenger samples and finds the major ions in near-constant ratios.
timeline.why: Salinity could be measured from a single ion.

timeline.title: Medicines from sponges
timeline.text: Werner Bergmann reports unusual nucleosides from a Caribbean sponge.
timeline.why: Inspired the cancer drug cytarabine and antivirals.

timeline.title: The ocean's limits
timeline.text: Roger Revelle and Hans Suess show the ocean will not absorb all fossil CO₂ quickly.
timeline.why: An early warning about rising atmospheric CO₂.

timeline.title: Hydrothermal vents
timeline.text: Scientists discover vents and their ecosystems near the Galápagos.
timeline.why: Life can run on chemical energy.

timeline.title: The garbage patch
timeline.text: Charles Moore draws attention to plastic accumulating in the North Pacific.
timeline.why: Ocean plastics became a global concern.

timeline.title: Ocean acidification
timeline.text: Ken Caldeira and Michael Wickett coin the term 'ocean acidification'.
timeline.why: Named a second major CO₂ problem.

timeline.title: A drug from a cone snail
timeline.text: Ziconotide, based on cone snail venom, is approved for severe pain.
timeline.why: A marine molecule becomes a medicine.

timeline.title: A drug from a sea squirt
timeline.text: Trabectedin, first isolated from a sea squirt, is approved in Europe for soft-tissue sarcoma.
timeline.why: Marine natural products reach cancer treatment.

quiz.q: What is the average salinity of seawater?
quiz.explain: Often written as 35 parts per thousand.

quiz.q: Which is the most abundant ion in seawater?
quiz.explain: About 19 g/kg of chloride against about 11 g/kg of sodium.

quiz.q: Why does acidification harm shell-building organisms?
options: It lowers the carbonate available to build calcium carbonate shells
It heats the water above what shells can survive
It adds salt that dissolves the shells
It removes all oxygen from the water
quiz.explain: Extra H⁺ ions combine with carbonate ions.

options: Chemosynthesis, using energy from chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide
Sunlight filtering down to the deep sea
Only plankton falling from the surface
Volcanic heat alone, with no chemistry involved
quiz.explain: Microbes oxidize sulfide and feed the whole ecosystem.

quiz.q: The cancer drug cytarabine was inspired by nucleosides found in…

quiz.explain: A peptide that blocks calcium channels in nerves.

quiz.q: Dittmar's principle of constant proportions means that…
options: The ratios of the major ions are nearly the same everywhere
All seas have the same temperature
quiz.explain: Total salinity varies; the ratios barely do.
They come from broken-down plastic, fibres and abrasion.

quiz.q: By about how much has ocean surface pH dropped since pre-industrial times?
quiz.explain: Because pH is logarithmic, 0.1 units is about a 26–30% rise in H⁺.

quiz.explain: It sampled seawater, sediments and life across the oceans.

quiz.q: Why does the ocean absorb CO₂?
options: CO₂ dissolves and reacts with water and carbonate
The ocean breathes it in like a living organism
Only because algae absorb it at the surface
Salt in the water attracts carbon atoms
quiz.explain: Chemistry and biology both move carbon into the sea.
